title: Weather Regression
text: My family has lived in both Arizona and Washington, so I pulled daily weather data (NOAA’s Global Surface Summary of the Day, through the GSODR package) for April 2023 from Phoenix Goodyear Airport and Renton Municipal Airport. How well does the daily minimum temperature predict the daily maximum, and does that relationship differ between the two cities?

title: Weather Regression
text: My family has lived in both Arizona and Washington, so I pulled daily weather data (NOAA’s Global Surface Summary of the Day, through the GSODR package) for April 2023 from Phoenix Goodyear Airport and Renton Municipal Airport. How well does the daily minimum temperature predict the daily maximum, and does that relationship differ between the two cities?

title: Weather Regression
text:
Model
\[
\hat{Y}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \beta_2 X_{i2} + \beta_3 X_{i1} X_{i2}
\]
where \(Y\) is the daily maximum temperature, \(X_1\) is the daily minimum temperature, and \(X_2\) is an indicator for Renton (Phoenix is the baseline). The \(\beta_2\) term lets the lines start at different heights, and the \(\beta_3\) interaction lets them have different slopes.
weather_lm_full <- lm(MAX ~ MIN + AIRPORT + MIN:AIRPORT, data = weather)

title: Weather Regression
text:
Results
The model fit 60 daily observations and explained about 92% of the variation in the daily maximum (adjusted \(R^2\) = 0.920).



Term
Estimate
p-value




Intercept (Phoenix)
17.5
< 0.0001


Minimum temperature (Phoenix slope)
0.914
< 0.0001


Renton shift in intercept
-9.919
< 0.0001


Renton shift in slope
0.436
0.043




In Phoenix, each 1°C rise in the minimum goes with about a 0.91°C rise in the maximum.
In Renton, the line starts about 9.9°C lower, and the slope is steeper at about 1.35°C per 1°C.

I checked all five regression assumptions (linearity, normal errors, constant variance, fixed X, and independent errors) with residual plots and judged the model appropriate. The result matches what the climates would suggest: Phoenix is hotter than Renton in April, and the minimum temperature carries more of the day’s range in Renton.

title: Comparing Models
text:
Q1: Three classifiers
I fit a decision tree, a random forest, and a gradient boosting classifier on the same training data and compared their classification reports and feature importances.



Model
Accuracy




Decision tree
0.89


Random forest
0.92


Gradient boosting
0.89



All three models agreed on the strongest predictors: one-story architecture, an attached garage, and home quality. Gradient boosting ranked the number of bathrooms above living area. I recommended the random forest because it had the best accuracy, precision, and recall.

title: Comparing Models
text:
Q2: Adding neighborhood data
I joined the neighborhood dataset to the housing data on the parcel number and re-ran the random forest. The top features did not change, and neighborhood itself was not an important feature. Even so, accuracy rose to 0.97, so I recommended this version of the model.

title: Comparing Models
text:
Q3: Predicting the year built
This is a regression problem, so I evaluated it with error measures instead of accuracy.



Model
R²
RMSE
MAE




Gradient boosting regressor
0.759

The residual plot for the first model showed it consistently underestimated the year for older homes and overestimated it for newer ones, so I called it a weak model. The random forest regressor cut the typical error roughly in half. It takes longer to run, but both finish in under a minute, so I recommended the random forest regressor.

title: Classifying Home Age
text: Can a model tell whether a home was built before 1980, using only features of the home such as architectural style, garage type, quality, and living area?

title: Classifying Home Age
text: Can a model tell whether a home was built before 1980, using only features of the home such as architectural style, garage type, quality, and living area?

title: Classifying Home Age
text:
Approach
I used a public housing dataset from the BYU-Idaho data science program (dwellings_ml). I dropped the identifier and year columns so the model could not see the answer directly, split the data 80/20 into training and test sets, and fit a decision tree classifier in scikit-learn.
x_features = df.drop(columns=["parcel", "abstrprd", "yrbuilt", "before1980"])
y_targets = df.before1980

train_data, test_data, train_targets, test_targets = train_test_split(
    x_features, y_targets, test_size=0.2
)

classifier = DecisionTreeClassifier()
classifier.fit(train_data, train_targets)

title: Classifying Home Age
text:
Results
The model correctly classified about 90% of the homes in the test set. I reported accuracy, precision, and recall, and explained each one in plain language:

Accuracy: of all test homes, the share the model labeled correctly.
Precision: of the homes the model labeled as built before (or after) 1980, the share that really were.
Recall: of the homes that really were built before (or after) 1980, the share the model found.

title: Classifying Home Age
text:
What drives the predictions
A one-story architectural style was the most important feature (importance 0.249), followed by an attached garage (0.126). Home quality and living area came next. Every other feature had an importance below 0.05.
I charted the importances with lets-plot to show the client which characteristics matter most.

title: Python: Confidence vs. Retail Sales
text:
A command-line program that asks whether consumer confidence and retail spending move together. The user enters two dates between January 1992 and March 2025, and the program reports how both measures changed over that period.
Data: a monthly consumer confidence index and monthly retail sales, with sources from FRED.

title: Python: Confidence vs. Retail Sales
text:
A command-line program that asks whether consumer confidence and retail spending move together. The user enters two dates between January 1992 and March 2025, and the program reports how both measures changed over that period.
Data: a monthly consumer confidence index and monthly retail sales, with sources from FRED.

title: Python: Confidence vs. Retail Sales
text:
What the program does

Reads the two CSV files into dictionaries keyed by date and merges them into one compound dictionary.
Validates the user’s input: the dates must parse as “Month, Year”, differ from each other, fall in order, and exist in the data.
Builds the date range and calculates each series’ percent change between the two dates.
Calculates the mean, standard deviation, and the Pearson correlation coefficient with NumPy.
Translates the correlation into a plain-English conclusion, from “almost no correlation” to “very strong correlation.”
Prints a formatted summary table with tabulate.

def write_conclusion(correl_coef):
    abs_correl_coef = abs(correl_coef)
    if abs_correl_coef <= 0.16:
        conclusion = "There is almost no correlation between retail sales and CCI in the given time period."
    elif abs_correl_coef <= 0.29:
        conclusion = "There is a very weak correlation between retail sales and CCI in the given time period."
    # ... thresholds continue up to "very strong" above 0.89

title: Python: Confidence vs. Retail Sales
text:
Skills practiced
Writing small, single-purpose functions with docstrings, reading files with the csv module, working with datetime, handling bad input, and testing the program with a companion test_ script.

title: SQL: Music Library Database
text:
Data integrity and changes

Converted the composer birth and death year columns to dates.
Added a CHECK constraint so a piece’s minimum performers can never exceed its maximum.
Renamed a table for consistency, dropped an unneeded column, and added a “Single Piece/No Book” entry.
Wrapped inserts and updates in transactions, including adding a new piece and linking it to a book.

title: SQL: Music Library Database
text:
Advanced queries

Every piece, book, and composer on a given shelf, using a five-table join.
The average difficulty of each piece across all of its parts, using AVG and GROUP BY.
The number of pieces in each book, ranked from most to fewest:

SELECT bhp.book_id AS "Book ID", b.book_title AS "Book Title", COUNT(*) AS "Num. of Pieces"
FROM book_has_piece AS bhp
  JOIN book AS b ON bhp.book_id = b.book_id
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 3 DESC;

title: SQL: Music Library Database
text:
Views

full_lib_overview shows each piece with its book, composer, genre, and whether it is in the performance repertoire.
perf_hist_overview lists each performance with its event, date, award, and the pieces played, using GROUP_CONCAT.

title: Holiday Cocoa Promotions (ANOVA)
text:
Approach
I built a consulting report in R (car, tidyverse, pander) from the company’s sales data.

Calculated revenue as units sold times actual price.
Grouped each week’s promotion depth into three levels: none, small (depth under 0.25), and medium (depth from 0.25 to 0.36).
Used ANOVA to compare revenue across promotion levels and regions.

title: Price of Promotion (Econometrics)
text:
Measuring the Price of Promotion: A Store-Level Analysis of Consumer Expenditure
Erral Asper, Kathryn Haroldsen, Taylor Landini, Mary Palmer, and Harrison Thomas (April 2026)

title: Price of Promotion (Econometrics)
text:
Question
Does promotional advertising push the prices consumers pay up or down? Economic theory points both ways: price-focused promotions can intensify competition, while brand-building advertising can reduce price sensitivity and support higher prices.

title: Price of Promotion (Econometrics)
text:
Data
We used the Dominick’s Finer Foods scanner database, compiled by the University of Chicago Booth School of Business from about 100 grocery stores from 1989 to 1994, and focused on the frozen dinner category.

Unbalanced panel of 19,306 store-item units over weeks 1 to 255, for 1,645,316 observations
Removed observations flagged as unreliable, prices of $0, and prices above $6 (over 99% of the data fell below that cutoff)
Promotions coded as Bonus Buy, Coupon, or Simple Price Reduction, compared with weeks with no recorded promotion

title: Price of Promotion (Econometrics)
text:
Method
Fixed effects regression with store-item fixed effects, so that each product in each store is compared only against itself across weeks. Model 1 regresses price on the three promotion types. Model 2 adds the retailer’s profit margin.

title: Price of Promotion (Econometrics)
text:
Findings
Relative to non-promotion weeks, average prices were lower by:



Promotion type
Average price difference




Bonus Buy
$0.11


Simple Price Reduction
$0.46


Coupon
$0.95




Coupons were the deepest discount and also produced the highest median sales volume.
Adding profit (Model 2) shrank the promotion coefficients to near zero. Because profit depends directly on price, we treated it as endogenous and based our conclusions on Model 1.
A Breusch-Pagan test (BP = 830.21, p < 0.01) found heteroskedasticity, so we used robust standard errors. Variance inflation factors near 1.0 showed no multicollinearity.

title: Price of Promotion (Econometrics)
text:
Limitations
The data are observational, cover one retailer and one time period, and record promotions imperfectly, so the results should not be read as causal or applied directly to modern online retail.

title: Merger Sales Dashboard
text:
What the data shows

Revenue growth has flattened. Total revenue across the period is $66.12M with $30.19M in gross profit and an average profit of $226.26 per sale. Quarterly revenue climbed from 2019 through 2022, which is why the page reads “profitable but plateauing.”
Margins are healthy but uneven. Gross profit margin rose from about 40% in 2019 to about 46% by the end of 2022, while clothing profit margins stood out as a concern.




Revenue, gross profit, and margin by year and quarter, with a table and bar chart toggle.



Younger customers drive sales. AdventureWorks’ main demographic is males ages 20 to 30, which lines up with GoBig’s customer base. Millennials and Gen Z lead revenue, although Gen Z revenue peaked in 2022 and has since fallen back below Millennials.




Quarterly revenue by generation.



Bikes carry the business. Bikes generate the most revenue and profit even with lower inventory, and they turn over inventory far faster than components.




Gross profit versus markup by product, with estimated inventory turnover by category.
